job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a room with my older brother Mateo in our parents' flat. My father drives long-haul trucks and my mother works at a pharmacy, so mornings are quiet. I spend the first hours on applications and a security training platform, then walk to local shops to sell them a basic IT and security check for 60 pounds. I use an AI assistant all day, for scripts, emails and learning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computing with a cyber security focus and passed with an average mark. My final project was a tool that spots odd traffic on a home router. I had no internship, and about 80 applications have brought two interviews and no offer, so I started my own small service while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means the world of work stays understandable, and people like my father can keep their jobs. At the shops I'd say the practical stuff still matters, like backups and passwords.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't fix my problem. Firms are choosy and a pass degree doesn't stand out. But the shop checks have brought in 300 pounds this month, so I'm not at zero, and that's the part that keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to ten shops a week and aim for five regular clients on a monthly plan, about 40 a month each. I'd get an entry security certificate for around 250 pounds, and keep applying to firms. I'd also ask my father to introduce me to the logistics firms he drives for, since they'd have IT needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, with an itch. I don't like waiting for someone to pick me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the shop owners say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most say they don't have time to think about security until something goes wrong. One bakery had its till frozen by a virus, and the owner told me she'd pay anything. That's my pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the itch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a proper first job, with people to learn from. Working alone is fine for now, but I don't know what I don't know.

A plateau means people like my father can keep their **jobs**.

Pay about **250 pounds** for an entry security certificate.
Ask my father to introduce me to the **logistics** firms he drives for.
feel: **Okay**, with an itch; I don't like waiting for someone to pick me.

fieldNote: Starting his own **small business** is the traditional work-first response.

Wants a **team** to learn from, recognising the limit of going alone.

steps.text: Visit ten local shops a week to sell security checks
Sign five shops to a monthly plan of about 40
Pay about 250 pounds for an entry security certificate
Ask his father to introduce him to logistics firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the way the market moves. Some jobs go and others appear. People who learn the tools and serve customers will be okay. I'd say governments should stay out of the way except for basic safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the junior coding and checking roles shrink, and I'd need to be better than a junior. But AI also creates new risks, like scams and weak systems, and small firms need someone to look after that. That's where I'm already working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on the shop service and add what AI can't easily do: being there, explaining, fixing the till on a busy Saturday. I'd use AI to do my own work faster, so I can serve more clients, and I'd build a simple monthly report I send them. I'd also take a cloud security course, and maybe hire a part-time helper once I reach ten clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and a bit pleased. It's a market with a gap in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the gap real, or a story you tell yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I have five paying clients, so it's real. But I'm small, and one big company could sell the same thing to my clients cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be the person who picks up the phone and knows their shop. People pay for someone they can ring, and I'd stay local.

steps.text: Use AI to speed up security checks and send monthly reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for the market to adjust on its own, and I'd say that surprises me, because I normally say leave it to the market. Some kind of safety net will be needed for the first couple of years, but I'd still say work comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one that worries me. If AI does thinking work better and cheaper in two years, my small business is in danger too, since big firms could sell cheap cyber checks run entirely by AI. My edge of being local would be real but thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the clients and move toward things that need a person in the room: installing, fixing, training staff. I'd save 300 a month, cut the certificate and course spending to the ones that count, and pick up hands-on jobs, like network cabling. I'd also look at partnering with an electrician. I'd stay with my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. I'd say wired, and I wouldn't sleep well for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why partner with an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the physical work comes three years after the thinking work. Cabling and fitting stay human longer. If I can sell a package, checks and cabling, I stay useful in the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To do the same. Mateo works in a warehouse, and I'd say learn the machines that are coming in, because someone has to keep them running.

A safety net will be needed for the first couple of years, but **work** comes first.
think: Big firms could sell cheap cyber checks run entirely by AI, so my small **business** is in danger.
My edge of being **local** would be real but thin.
do: Move toward things that need a person in the room: **installing**, fixing, training staff.
Save **300 a month** and keep only the courses that count.
Partner with an **electrician** to sell checks and cabling together.
feel: **Tense**, wired, and I wouldn't sleep well for a while.
S2.quote: Cabling and fitting stay human longer. If I can sell a package, checks and cabling, I stay useful in the gap.
fieldNote: Admits his usual **free-market** view bends in the fastest case.
Uses the three-year **robot** lag as a business plan.
Includes his **brother** in the plan, though only briefly.

steps.text: Partner with an electrician to sell checks and cabling
Learn network cabling and fitting for shops
Save 300 a month and keep only key courses
Tell his brother Mateo to learn the warehouse machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the market to respond, and for people to retrain. I'd say employers should do their share and train people, and I'd say the young should start something of their own if they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's an opportunity and a risk. I could build a real business in five years, with clients and staff. Or I could be undercut by a big firm. I'd say sixty-forty it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for 20 clients, hire a helper, and invest in a small stock of equipment. I'd save 250 a month, keep applying for a security job to get the training, and learn the new AI security tools as they come. I'd also ask my father to be a guarantor if I need a small business loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little scared. I think I do better with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sixty-forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I have a real client list and a trade, but I'm 23, with no firm behind me. If I'm lucky, it takes off. If not, I get a job and the experience still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a business loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Equipment and a van, not much. I wouldn't borrow more than I can pay off in two years. My father taught me that.

Employers should do their share and **train** people.

steps.text: Grow the client list to 20 local shops

Keep applying for a junior security job for training
Save 250 a month for equipment and a van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people who start early will do well. I'd say the best thing the state can do is keep rules simple, and the best thing families can do is save and train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'm not worried. A decade is enough to build something solid, get a security job, maybe both. I'd probably have my own firm by then, with a few staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the shop service, take a security analyst job for the training and keep the business as a side line. I'd save 300 a month toward a flat, learn new AI tools every few months and help my parents with their retirement planning. I might marry in that time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a little excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the main thing that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad few years early on, where I can't get a break. I'd rather have the first job soon so I'm not behind. A decade is long, but the first two years matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope to be in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who runs a small firm and keeps three or four people in work. That's the dream, and I'd say it's a fair one.

The state should keep rules **simple**, and families should save and train.

fieldNote: Calm built on a **working** business, not just hope.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because big firms could undercut me before I have a name. I'd have a few clients and not much money. What would help is a way to get a first job with training, clear rules about AI sold to small businesses and a short loan I can trust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to see that young people like me aren't waiting around. We're trying things. We just need the first door to open a little.

headlineQuote: Young people like me aren't waiting around. We're trying things. We just need the first door to open a little.
portrait: Nikhil is a 23-year-old **cyber security** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 80 applications sent.
He shares a room with his brother Mateo and sells **IT and security checks** to local shops for 60 pounds.
He is traditional, free-market, curious and uses AI every day, so he is **adaptive** by habit.
His mood stays uneasy in most worlds, **anxious** at two years and calm when he has ten.
He bets on **local trust**, a small firm and family caution about debt, with a job as the fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, because big firms could undercut him before he has a name.
whatWouldHelp: A first job with **training**, clear rules on AI sold to small firms and a short, trusted loan.
